traveler: Ibrahim ibn Adham (Ebrahim b. Adham b. Mansur b. Yazid al-'Ijli)
title: The Palace Door to the Byzantine Sea: the Prince of Balkh, the Shepherd's Coat, and the Seven Graves
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kufa, the tribe takes the eastern road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source dates the Banu Ijl migration out of Kufa, only that it precedes his birth at Balkh. The year shown is a placeholder inside a generation-wide window.
stops.campa: The Banu Ijl ride east out of Kufa with the armies of the conquest, and keep going, past the Zagros, past Nishapur, past Merv, until the road ends at Balkh under the Hindu Kush. They settle there as a garrison people among Persians, holding land and keeping their Arabic and their tribal name. Four or five generations later a boy of that stock is born in the city, and the storytellers will make him its prince. His great-grandfather's people were soldiers out of Iraq. The throne he is said to renounce belonged to somebody else's ancestors.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kufa, city the family left for Khurasan generations before his birth
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1, 'EBRAHIM B. ADHAM' ('born to a notable Kufan family in Balkh')
English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (Banu Tamim / Banu Ijl migration from Kufa)

stops.name: Balkh, the birth of Ibrahim ibn Adham
stops.date_confidence: traditional; 100 AH converts to 718-719 CE, so the standard 'c. 718' is arithmetically sound, but no source gives a month or a day
stops.campa: In the hundredth year of the Hijra a son is born at Balkh to Adham son of Mansur son of Yazid of the Banu Ijl, and is named Ibrahim. The city is old past reckoning: Zoroaster died at its fire-altar, Alexander married Roxana in its citadel, and five centuries after this birth Baha ud-Din Walad will carry the infant Rumi out through its gates ahead of the Mongols. Others are carried out of Balkh ahead of an army. This one will walk out on his own legs and never come back.
suggested_refs: The walled site of Balkh, mother of cities, in the year 100 of the Hijra
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1, 'EBRAHIM B. ADHAM' (correct nasab: b. Adham b. Mansur b. Yazid b. Jaber 'Ejli)
English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham'
Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم

stops.name: Balkh, the citadel and the governorship
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source dates any tenure of his at Balkh, and Iranica treats the whole abdication cycle as Sufi legend attached at most to the governorship
stops.campa: The Bala Hisar stands at the north of the walled site, oval, a mile and a half by a mile, and whoever holds it holds Balkh. Tradition seats Ibrahim there as king. The encyclopaedias that treat him as a historical man seat him at most in a governorship, and call the rest a Sufi legend. Both accounts agree on one thing: he had something to give up, and gave it up. What differs is only the size of it, a crown or an office, and the tellers who came later had no use whatever for an office.
suggested_refs: The Bala Hissar of Balkh, oval citadel at the north of the site, roughly 1,500 by 1,000 metres
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1 (abdication stories classed as Sufi legends about the governorship)
English Wikipedia, 'Balkh' (dimensions and position of the Bala Hissar)

stops.name: Balkh, the palace and the years of plenty
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; Attar describes the opulence without fixing a year, and no eighth-century source describes it at all
stops.campa: He lives as the son of a notable house lives: horses, hunting dogs, servants, the hospitality that keeps a family's standing in a frontier city. Attar, writing five centuries later, describes the opulence in detail because the story needs a height to fall from. No contemporary of Ibrahim describes it at any length. The palace in the Tadhkirat al-Awliya is built out of the requirements of the narrative, and it is furnished very well. The man who walks out of it walks out of a room no eighth-century witness ever entered.
suggested_refs: Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter ten, the princely establishment at Balkh
sources: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (via secondary summaries; Arberry's translation returned HTTP 401 on the full-text endpoint)

stops.name: The hunting ground outside Balkh, the voice in the chase
stops.date_confidence: contradiction carried, not resolved: English-language sources place the awakening and abdication c. 750, but rabia.journey.json dates the Mecca-road meeting to 5 April 737 after fourteen years of walking, which requires a renunciation before 723. The earlier date is used here to keep the atlas internally consistent; the c. 750 tradition stands unrefuted.
stops.campa: He is riding down a gazelle in the open country outside the city when a voice speaks, and the versions divide over whose it is: the animal's, or nobody's, or God's own. Burton, who set the sentence into English, calls it legend and names no authority earlier than legend. The structure is older than Balkh and wider than Islam: a young man of rank goes out for pleasure and meets, in the middle of his pleasure, the fact of his own death. The chase stops. The gazelle is not recorded as having been killed.
stops.quote: Man! it is not for this that Allah made thee!
stops.quote_source: Richard F. Burton, Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage to Al-Madinah and Meccah, vol. III, footnote to ch. XXVIII
suggested_refs: The open hunting country north of Balkh; no source fixes the site more closely than 'while hunting'
sources: Burton, Personal Narrative, vol. III (Wikisource full text)
Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم
English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham'

stops.name: Near Balkh, Khidr on the road
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; the day shown is a sequence marker only, and the Khidr version and the voice version are alternatives to each other, not consecutive events
stops.campa: The other version puts no voice in the air but a man on the road: Khidr, the green one, the deathless guide who appears where he is needed and is gone once he is understood. He comes twice, in the fuller tellings, because once was not enough. The two accounts of this morning cannot both be true and no source reconciles them. What survives in every telling is the arithmetic that follows. He does not go home, weigh the matter, and decide. He turns around where he is standing.
suggested_refs: The Khidr cycle in early Sufi hagiography, in which the green guide appears twice to those who refuse the first warning
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (Khidr appears twice)
Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم (voice version, given as an alternative)

stops.name: Balkh, the shepherd's coat at the palace door
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; the Arabic tradition alone preserves the clothes-exchange, and English summaries give the renunciation without it
stops.campa: A shepherd is passing the gate in a coat of coarse wool. Ibrahim takes off what he is wearing, hands it over, and puts on the shepherd's garment in the street, in front of whoever is watching. The Arabic tradition keeps this exchange; the English summaries drop it. It is the one gesture in the whole legend that costs a witness something, because the shepherd now owns the clothes and has to be seen wearing them afterward. Ibrahim walks out of Balkh dressed as the poorest man he could find at short notice.
suggested_refs: The clothes-exchange with the shepherd, preserved in the Arabic tradition and absent from English summaries
sources: Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم
English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (renunciation without the clothes-exchange)

stops.name: The open country beyond Balkh, the walk out without provisions
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; no source fixes a route out of Khurasan, and the year is inferred from the Mecca arrival working backward
stops.campa: He crosses open desert on foot carrying nothing, which is the whole point of it: trust in providence means nothing while a bag of bread hangs at your shoulder. No source fixes a route. He is heading generally west and generally south, toward the House at Mecca, along roads Khurasani pilgrims have used since the conquest and will keep using. Abu Yazid of Bastam takes the same turns a century later, Bastam first and then the Iraqi cities, and Attar of Nishapur takes them again after that.
suggested_refs: The Khurasan pilgrim road west out of Balkh, used unchanged from the conquest to the Mongols
sources: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (traditional; via secondary summaries)

segments.name: The Desert Road and the House

stops.name: Nishapur, the road through the city that will keep him
stops.date_confidence: unsupported as biography: no source places Ibrahim ibn Adham at Nishapur. The stop is kept for the road and for what the city does to his story five centuries later, and the campa says so.
stops.campa: The Khurasan road runs through Nishapur, and he passes through it as any traveler does, leaving nothing behind him. No source places him in this city; the pin is here for a different reason. Five centuries on, a druggist of Nishapur named Farid al-Din Attar will sit down in this city and write the life of Ibrahim ibn Adham as the tenth of ninety-six, and every retelling that follows runs through his pages. The city with no record of the man is where his story gets manufactured.
suggested_refs: Shadiyakh, the southern quarter of Nishapur, near the tomb of Attar
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Nishapur' (coordinates; Shadiyakh in the southern district)

stops.name: The Nejd crossing, two prostrations at every step
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the fourteen-year crossing is a hagiographic figure, not a measured duration, and the pin is an approximation on the central Arabian route
stops.campa: He crosses the waste of central Arabia toward the Hijaz, praying two prostrations at every step, which is how the legend accounts for fourteen years spent on a journey a caravan makes in weeks. The arithmetic is the point of the story. No teller has ever treated it as a difficulty. Nothing is recorded of where he slept or what he ate on the way. Rabia of Basra is crossing the same desert in these same years by another road and another discipline, and the two of them are about to arrive at one place in one hour.
suggested_refs: The central Arabian pilgrim crossing, walked rather than ridden in the hagiographic accounts
sources: Sufi hagiographic tradition as recorded in Jami, Nafahat al-Uns

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba, the years of circling
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; the month shown places him at the House shortly before the meeting the atlas already dates to 5 April 737
stops.campa: He arrives at the House and circles it, and goes on circling it, for as long as the tellers need him to. Here Khidr comes back a third time in some versions and teaches him the greatest name of God, though the encyclopaedias that confirm Khidr in the conversion story do not put him at Mecca at all. Hallaj will keep a year-long vigil on these same stones a century and a half later and be crucified for what he says about them. Neither man leaves these stones the way he arrived at them.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Sacred Mosque, canonical pin of the atlas at 21.4225, 39.8262
sources: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (traditional)
English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (Khidr confirmed in the conversion, not fixed at Mecca)

stops.name: Outskirts of Mecca, the Kaaba goes out to meet Rabia
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date is inherited byte-for-byte from rabia.journey.json so that the two files stage one event, and it sits thirteen years earlier than the c. 750 abdication the English sources give
stops.campa: He comes up the last stretch of road and the House is not there. The Kaaba has left its foundation and gone out to meet a woman approaching from the other direction. He runs, and finds Rabia of Basra arriving, and the House already back on its base behind her. Fourteen years of prostrations at every step, and a woman he has never met has drawn the building itself out onto the road. The motif is told of several other saints too, which the retellings do not always trouble to mention.
stops.quote: You have spent fourteen years in crossing the desert in ritual prayer; I have crossed it in personal supplication.
stops.quote_source: Sufi hagiographic tradition, recorded in later redactions of Attar and in Jami's Nafahat al-Uns
suggested_refs: The meeting of Rabia and Ibrahim ibn Adham on the Mecca road, a set scene in later Persian miniature painting

stops.name: Mecca, the prayer about the gnat
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source; the prayer is attached to him without occasion, and the year here only keeps it inside the Mecca years
stops.campa: A prayer of his is kept in Ghazali's digest, and the same prayer, or one very like it, turns up in the 1911 Britannica article on Sufism in wholly different English, where the eight Paradises are little beside the honour done him. Nobody names the Arabic behind either rendering, so it cannot be settled whether these are two translations of one sentence or two sentences. What both versions do is identical work. They put a price on heaven, and find it cheap.
stops.quote: O God! In my eyes heaven itself is less than a gnat in comparison with the love of Thee and the joy of Thy remembrance which thou hast granted me.
stops.quote_source: Al-Ghazali, The Alchemy of Happiness, trans. Claud Field, ch. VIII
suggested_refs: The variant rendering in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article 'Sufiism': 'the eight Paradises are little beside the honour which Thou hast done unto me'
sources: Al-Ghazali, The Alchemy of Happiness, trans. Claud Field (Wikisource)
1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sufiism' (Wikisource; no translator named)

stops.name: Mecca, al-Fudayl ibn Iyad and the disputed direction
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source dates the meeting, and the two men's own dates (Fudayl b. 720s, d. 803; Ibrahim b. 718) make Fudayl the younger man and the survivor by decades
stops.campa: He meets al-Fudayl ibn Iyad at Mecca, and the sources cannot agree which of the two is the teacher. One Wikipedia article makes Ibrahim the student; the article on Fudayl himself makes Fudayl the master who taught Ibrahim. The only support for either is a Chishti hagiography compiled in India six hundred years afterward. Fudayl was born in the 720s and died in 803, which makes him the younger man and Ibrahim's survivor by decades. The chain of transmission runs, and nobody can say which way.
suggested_refs: Siyar ul Auliya i Chisht, 1884 Delhi reprint, sole support for the discipleship and not directly consulted
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (taught by al-Fudayl, per Chishti records)
English Wikipedia, 'Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad' (al-Fudayl taught Ibrahim ibn Adham)

Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1 (does not mention Fudayl at all)

stops.name: Balkh, the tribe strikes camp
stops.date_confidence: attested only as a terminus: Iranica says the migration happened before 137 AH, which is 754 CE. The year shown sits inside that window; the day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: The other account of how he left Khurasan has no gazelle in it and no shepherd. Iranica says he migrated with his tribe from Khorasan to Syria before the year 137, which is 754. That is a whole Arab settler group moving west together with its livestock and its households, for the reasons a tribe has: land, taxes, the frontier, the wars. In that version he renounces nothing at Balkh. He goes where his people go, and becomes an ascetic somewhere at the far end of the road.
suggested_refs: Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1: 'migrated with his tribe from Khorasan to Syria before 137/754'
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1, 'EBRAHIM B. ADHAM' (via Wayback snapshot 20260414123119)
Contradiction flagged against the hagiographic solitary-flight account, not resolved

stops.name: The Euphrates crossing, into Bilad al-Sham
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source describes the route or the crossing, and the pin marks the standard Khurasan-to-Syria road rather than an attested place
stops.campa: The road out of Khurasan runs the length of the Iranian plateau and comes down at last to the Euphrates, where the country changes and the Byzantine world starts to be a thing you can smell. Whether he crossed alone with a staff or in the middle of a moving tribe, he crossed here or within a few days' ride of here. Nothing is recorded of the crossing itself. The two versions of his life, the legend's and the encyclopaedia's, stand on the same bank at this point and do not speak to each other.
suggested_refs: The middle Euphrates crossings on the Khurasan-to-Syria road, unnamed in every source on his life
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (migration to Syria)
Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1
Gap recorded: no source names a route or a crossing

stops.name: Bilad al-Sham, the settling that settles nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested as a terminus ante quem (before 137 AH = 754 CE, per Iranica); English sources give the looser 'around 750'
stops.campa: He settles into Syria and does not settle anywhere in it. The life he takes up is semi-nomadic: no house kept for long, no fixed circle of students, no post, no patron. The sources say Syria and then stop; they name almost no towns and fix almost no years. Everything about the next twenty-odd years is known in kind and unknown in place. He grinds grain, he works orchards, he refuses alms, he moves on. That is the entire documentary record of the longest stretch of his life.
suggested_refs: Bilad al-Sham in the 750s, the Umayyad heartland newly under Abbasid rule
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham'
Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم
Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1

stops.name: Bilad al-Sham, the mill and the grain
stops.date_confidence: attested as practice, unlocated and undated; both Arabic and English sources describe the grain-grinding and neither attaches it to a town or a year
stops.campa: He hires himself out to grind grain. A man said to have owned a city works a handmill for a day's wage, and what he buys with it is ownership: bread earned by his own arms belongs to him in a way that alms and inheritance never will. He will not beg. He will not draw on what the family had. Every account of him in Syria, Arabic and English alike, agrees on this refusal, and not one of them attaches it to a named town, so the mill stands wherever you please in Syria.
suggested_refs: The labor ethic of the early Khurasani ascetics: manual wages taken, alms and inheritance refused
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham'
Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم
Gap recorded: the sources give the labor and withhold every location

stops.name: The coast of Syria, the orchards and the harvest wage
stops.date_confidence: attested as practice, unlocated and undated; the coastal pin is chosen for the orchard country and is not named in any source
stops.campa: North of the Lebanon the coastal strip runs green under the mountains, orchards and terraces stepping down to the sea, and there is seasonal work in them for anyone who will do it. He harvests and he gardens, and he is paid to guard another man's fruit crop until it comes off the trees. The tradition preserves the labor and loses the employers, so nobody knows whose trees they were. The sea he is working beside is the one he will eventually put out onto with a raiding fleet, and from which, in the account most often repeated, he does not come back.
suggested_refs: The orchard terraces of the Syrian coastal range, seasonal work for wandering ascetics
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (orchards, harvesting, gardening)
Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم

stops.name: A cell in the Syrian country, Simeon and the seventy years
stops.date_confidence: undated and unlocated; the source gives the dialogue and says only 'in his cell', naming no mountain, no monastery and no year
stops.campa: Somewhere in Syria he goes into a Christian monk's cell and asks the man a question. The source gives the dialogue and gives no location: no mountain, no monastery, no road leading to it. Seventy years in one room, the monk answers. Four centuries earlier, in the Egyptian desert, Anthony had begun the discipline this monk is at the far end of, and the Muslim ascetic who walked out of a palace has come here to be taught by it. He does not argue with the monk about religion. He asks him how it is done.
stops.quote: I visited him in his cell, and said to him, 'Father Simeon, how long hast thou been here?' 'For seventy years,' he answered.
stops.quote_source: Cyril Glasse, The Concise Encyclopedia of Islam (1989), p. 178, quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham'
suggested_refs: The monk Simeon (Sham'un) in his cell; the location given by the pass as Mount Lebanon is an invention, corrected here to unlocated
sources: Cyril Glasse, The Concise Encyclopedia of Islam (1989), p. 178, via English Wikipedia

stops.name: The same cell, one chickpea a night
stops.date_confidence: undated; the day is a sequence marker continuing the same conversation, which no source dates at all
stops.campa: The monk tells him what he eats and what he is paid for it: a single chickpea after dark, and one day a year when the people come out to decorate his cell and walk around it in procession. Then he sends Ibrahim away with an instruction, that a Hanifite should endure the labor of a year for the glory of eternity. The words reach us through a 1989 encyclopedia that names no medieval source behind them. The trail stops there. It is the plainest thing anybody in the whole record ever says to him.
stops.quote: Every night, one chickpea...They come to me one day in every year and adorn my cell and process about it, so doing me reverence.
stops.quote_source: Cyril Glasse, The Concise Encyclopedia of Islam (1989), p. 178, quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham'
suggested_refs: Simeon's closing exhortation: 'Do thou, O Hanifite, endure the labor of a year for the glory of eternity'
sources: Cyril Glasse, The Concise Encyclopedia of Islam (1989), p. 178, via English Wikipedia
Note: the ellipsis stands in the extracted text; the unabridged wording was not independently checked

stops.name: Gaza, the southern limit of the Syrian range
stops.date_confidence: attested as a limit, undated; English Wikipedia says he travelled 'as far south as Gaza' and names no building, no occasion and no year
stops.campa: His wandering carries him down the coast as far as Gaza, on the edge of the Egyptian desert, where the Syria of the sources runs out. Nothing is recorded of what he did there and no source names a building in the town. It is not the southernmost ground he ever stood on; Mecca lies eleven hundred kilometres further down. It is only the far end of the country he spent his working life crossing, the last town before the road turns into Sinai and stops being Sham.
suggested_refs: Gaza on the Byzantine-Egyptian frontier zone, the southern edge of Bilad al-Sham
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' ('as far south as Gaza')
Correction recorded: the pass named the Great Mosque of Gaza, which no source gives, and called Gaza his southernmost point, which Mecca contradicts

stops.name: Somewhere in Syria, the stone turned over
stops.date_confidence: undated and unlocated; Hujwiri tells it in the eleventh century as an anecdote already old in his own time
stops.campa: He finds a stone with writing on it telling him to turn it over, and he turns it over, and reads the sentence on the other side. Hujwiri, writing in the eleventh century, already hands it on as a story that reached him old. Three hundred years after the man died, it was already something people had heard before. The rebuke cut into the stone is aimed at a scholar and lands on everybody. He is the one who reports it, so he is the one it was written for.
stops.quote: Thou dost not practise what thou knowest; why, then, dost thou seek what thou knowest not?
stops.quote_source: Ali b. Uthman al-Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. R. A. Nicholson
suggested_refs: Hujwiri's Kashf al-Mahjub, eleventh-century Persian handbook of Sufism, earliest reachable carrier of the stone anecdote
sources: Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. Nicholson (archive.org, item kashfalmahjub00usmauoft, djvu full text)

stops.name: The Syrian marches, the years of ghazw
stops.date_confidence: attested as activity, undated and unlocated; neither Arabic nor English accounts name a battle, a commander or a year for the frontier campaigning
stops.campa: The frontier with Byzantium runs through the passes north of Antioch, and every summer raiding parties cross it in both directions. He goes on campaign. The renunciant who would not take alms takes a place in the line, and the sources on both sides of the tradition record it without embarrassment: asceticism in this generation does not exclude the frontier, it includes it. Neither the Arabic nor the English accounts name a battle, a commander, or a year for any part of it.
suggested_refs: The Byzantine-Arab frontier of the 760s and 770s, campaigned every summer from the Syrian marches
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (frontier and naval activity in his final period)
Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم

stops.name: Jableh, the muster on the coast
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source names a port of embarkation. Jableh is chosen because Jableh is where the strongest burial tradition puts him.
stops.campa: In his last years he is at sea. The Syrian coast fits out ships for raids against Byzantine islands, and he sails on one of them, an old man in a fleet. Abu Nu'aym al-Isfahani, writing in the tenth or eleventh century, is the earliest source anyone can name for this, not the twelfth-century Ibn Asakir the summaries usually credit. The town he sailed from is nowhere recorded. Jableh stands here because Jableh is where they say he came back to, in the ground.
suggested_refs: Abu Nu'aym al-Isfahani, Hilyat al-awliya vii, 388, earliest named source for the campaign death
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham', footnoting Abu Nu'aym, Hilyat al-awliya vii, 388
Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1 (campaign death grounded in Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Asakir jointly)
Correction recorded: the pass attributed the campaign report to Ibn Asakir alone

stops.name: The eastern Mediterranean, the raid against the islands
stops.date_confidence: disputed four ways: 161, 162, 165 or 166 AH, i.e. 777-778, 778-779, c. 782, or 782-783 CE. Arabic Wikipedia prints 162 and miscomputes it as 776, then cites 161 as an alternative two clauses later; English Wikipedia gives c. 165, Iranica 166. Not resolved.
stops.campa: The fleet goes out against the islands. No source names the island, the fleet, or the enemy commander, and the year is disputed four ways: 161, 162, 165 or 166 of the Hijra, which is 777, 778, 782 or 783. Arabic Wikipedia gives 162 and then miscalculates it as 776, and contradicts itself two clauses further down the page. This atlas takes 778 and prints the whole spread beside it. Somewhere in this water, in one of those years, the campaign that kills him begins.
suggested_refs: The Abbasid naval raids on Byzantine islands in the 160s of the Hijra, none of them named in any account of his death
sources: Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم (162 AH, glossed wrongly as 776)
English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (c. 165 AH / c. 782)
Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/1 (d. 166; campaign-death range 160-166 AH)

stops.name: An unnamed island, the bow strung at the end
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the anecdote is undated and untraced, and the month here only follows the campaign year the atlas has chosen
stops.campa: He is dying, on campaign, and he asks the men around him to string his bow. They string it, and he takes it in his hand, and dies holding it. The anecdote is repeated everywhere in the Arabic tradition and traced to nobody. A man who gave away a throne to walk barefoot across Asia ends with a weapon in his fist on a beach whose name nobody wrote down. The abandoned throne and the strung bow sit in one life without friction. Both are in every version, and no teller has ever found them contradictory.
suggested_refs: The strung-bow death anecdote, repeated across the Arabic biographical tradition without attribution
sources: Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم

stops.name: An island under Byzantium, the grave Ibn Asakir names
stops.date_confidence: attested as a tradition, undated and unlocated; Ibn Asakir wrote in the twelfth century, some three and a half centuries after the event
stops.campa: They bury him where he falls, on the island, and Ibn Asakir records it three and a half centuries later. This is the only one of the seven grave traditions that Ibn Asakir is actually cited for, though the summaries attach his name to most of them. It is also the only one with a body and a battle behind it. The other six have a shrine and a town's pride. Being the best-sourced grave has not made it the grave anybody visits. There is nothing there to visit.
suggested_refs: Ibn Asakir, Ta'rikh madinat Dimashq, sole source cited for the island burial
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham', 'Purported graves' section, citing Ibn Asakir
Correction recorded: the pass credited Ibn Asakir with the Tyre, Baghdad and Jerusalem claims as well

stops.name: Jableh, the mosque of Sultan Ibrahim ibn Adham
stops.date_confidence: the tomb tradition is old and continuous; the mosque's own foundation date is not given in any reachable source, and the year here marks the tradition's start, not the building's
stops.campa: The Syrian coast keeps him. A mosque at Jableh holds a tomb under his name and has held it for as long as anybody has bothered to write the town down. This is the shrine pilgrims actually go to. It answers the question where is he buried with a door you can walk through and a floor you can sit on. It is also flatly incompatible with the death at sea the same Arabic sources give three paragraphs earlier. The town has never found this a difficulty worth raising.
suggested_refs: The Mosque of Sultan Ibrahim ibn Adham at Jableh, on the Syrian coast; not to be confused with the mosque of the same name at Beit Hanina
sources: Arabic Wikipedia, إبراهيم بن أدهم
English Wikipedia, 'Jableh' ('It contains the tomb and mosque of Ibrahim Bin Adham')

stops.name: Tyre, a second grave on the same coast
stops.date_confidence: attested as a tradition only, undated; Encyclopedia of Islam III, 985 carries it, and that volume was not directly consulted
stops.campa: Ninety kilometres south, Tyre claims him too, on the authority of the Encyclopedia of Islam. Nothing else in the record puts him at Tyre: not a residence, not a season of work, not a passage through the town. The grave arrives with no life attached to it. Two Levantine ports on one stretch of coast keep two tombs of a single man who is elsewhere reported buried on an island, and the sources record all three without ranking any of them above the others.
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia of Islam vol. III, p. 985, cited for the Tyre, Baghdad and 'city of the prophet Lot' burial claims
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham', 'Purported graves', citing Encyclopedia of Islam III, 985
Correction recorded: the pass added a Tyre residence and manual labor, for which no source exists

stops.name: Baghdad, a grave in a city younger than the man
stops.date_confidence: attested as a tradition only, undated; the arithmetic constraint is firm, since Baghdad was founded in 762
stops.campa: Baghdad claims a grave, which is arithmetically awkward: the city was founded in 762, when Ibrahim was already in his forties and already in Syria. If he is buried here he reached a capital still under construction for most of his life, in the last two decades of it, and no account describes the journey. The Encyclopedia of Islam carries the claim anyway. Hallaj will be crucified in this city a century and a half later, and nobody will ever dispute where he ended.
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia of Islam vol. III, p. 985; the Adhamiyya quarter anchor used by earlier summaries dates only to 985-986 CE and is dropped
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham', 'Purported graves'

stops.name: Jerusalem, the cave of Jeremiah
stops.date_confidence: uncited: English Wikipedia carries this burial tradition with no footnote of any kind, and the tag is downgraded accordingly
stops.campa: North of the Damascus Gate there is a grotto they call Jeremiah's, and one tradition puts Ibrahim ibn Adham inside it. This is the weakest of the seven claims: the encyclopaedia carries it with no citation at all, and the research that reached this atlas confused the grotto with Zedekiah's Cave, a quarry a few hundred metres away under the city wall. A grave with no source and, until this pass, no correct address. It is listed because the record lists it.
suggested_refs: Jeremiah's Grotto, north of the Damascus Gate; distinct from Zedekiah's Cave, the quarry under the wall between the Damascus and Herod Gates
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham', 'Purported graves' (uncited line)
English Wikipedia, 'Zedekiah's Cave' (no connection to Jeremiah or to Ibrahim ibn Adham)

stops.name: Sur, Oman, the shrine no source explains
stops.date_confidence: undated and unexplained; the shrine is asserted in the sources without narrative, and is probably a late local attribution
stops.campa: On the coast of Oman, two thousand kilometres from anywhere he is known to have stood, the town of Sur keeps a shrine of Sultan Ibrahim ibn Adham. No source explains how it got there. No account of his travels reaches the Arabian Sea at all. The connection is asserted and never argued, in every place that mentions it, and this atlas can do no better than say so: it is a gap in the shape of a building. Seven graves now, on three seas, and the tradition has never chosen between them.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Sultan Ibrahim ibn Adham at Sur al-Batha, Oman; and the seventh claim, 'the city of the prophet Lot', unlocated and unpinned
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (Oman shrine asserted without supporting narrative)

stops.name: Baghdad, a verse addressed to a caliph who is not yet caliph
stops.date_confidence: impossible as attributed: Harun al-Rashid becomes caliph in 786, at least four years after the latest death date offered for Ibrahim and eight after the likeliest. Either the attribution is wrong or every death date is.
stops.campa: A poem survives in English addressed by Ibrahim ben Adham to Harun al-Rashid, telling a caliph that religion's jewels will tear straight through a robe cut for pleasure. Harun becomes caliph in 786, at least four years after the latest date anyone offers for Ibrahim's death and eight after the likeliest. Either the attribution is wrong or every death date is. Nobody has produced the Arabic; the chain stops at a Victorian anthology, and the poem goes on being his.
stops.quote:
Religion's gems can ne'er adorn / The flimsy robe by pleasure worn; / Its feeble texture soon would tear, / And give those jewels to the air.

Thrice happy they who seek th' abode / Of peace and pleasure, in their God! / Who spurn the world, its joys despise, / And grasp at bliss beyond the skies.
stops.quote_source: 'To the Caliph Harun-al-Rashid,' attributed to Ibrahim Ben Adham, trans. Epiphanius Wilson, in Arabian Literature
suggested_refs: Epiphanius Wilson's Arabian Literature anthology, sole carrier of the verse epistle in English and the end of its traceable chain
sources: Wikisource, 'To the Caliph Harun-al-Rashid', author given as Ibrahim Ben Adham, trans. Epiphanius Wilson
Correction recorded: the pass cited a Persian-literature anthology and ran the two quatrains together as prose

stops.name: Balkh, Shaqiq al-Balkhi and the chain of teachers
stops.date_confidence: attested only as Shaqiq's death year (194 AH = 810 CE, which converts correctly); the discipleship itself is undated and unlocated, and English Wikipedia gives it as 'tradition makes him the disciple'
stops.campa: Back at the city he left, a man named Shaqiq is called his most famous student, and dies in 810. Where or when the two of them met is recorded nowhere; the discipleship is a link in a chain of names, and nothing in the record makes it an event in a place. Shaqiq turns up elsewhere in this atlas at Rabia's deathbed in Basra, beside Hasan and Malik ibn Dinar. Through him the Khurasani line runs forward into every Sufi order that later needs an eighth-century ancestor, and Ibrahim becomes the ancestor.
suggested_refs: The silsila claims of the later Sufi orders, which run their chains back through Shaqiq al-Balkhi to Ibrahim ibn Adham
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Shaqiq al-Balkhi' ('Tradition makes him the disciple of Ibrahim ibn Adham')

stops.name: Azimpur, Dhaka, the later namesake
stops.date_confidence: attested as a local tradition and as a namesake; 281 AH converts to 894-895 CE, more than a century after any death date offered for the Balkh ascetic
stops.campa: In Old Dhaka a mausoleum and a mosque are kept for a Hazrat Ibrahim Adham said to have settled here in the year 281, which is 894, more than a century after the Balkh ascetic died on his island. This is a later namesake and the sources say so plainly, in a passage set under a heading that says so as well. The confusion is not anywhere in the record; it lives entirely in the retellings. Bengal has its own Ibrahim Adham and has never needed the Khurasani one in order to keep him.
suggested_refs: The mazar and mosque of Hazrat Ibrahim Adham at Azimpur, Old Dhaka
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham', section 'Namesakes' ('Among the later namesakes of Ibrahim ibn Adham...')
Correction recorded: the pass claimed the sources leave the identity unresolved; they resolve it explicitly

stops.name: Beit Hanina, the second mosque of his name
stops.date_confidence: attested by an on-site inscription dating the building to 336 AH, which is 947-948 CE
stops.campa: An inscription in the wall of a mosque at Beit Hanina, north of Jerusalem, dates the building to the year 336, which is 947 or 948. It carries his name. It is not the Jableh mosque, though the two share a title and are constantly confused with each other, and it is two centuries the older. Two standing buildings, one in Syria and one in Palestine, are called the Mosque of Sultan Ibrahim ibn Adham, and the research that reached this atlas knew about only one of them.
suggested_refs: The Sultan Ibrahim Ibn Adham Mosque at Beit Hanina, East Jerusalem, completed 336 AH per its own inscription
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Sultan Ibrahim Ibn Adham Mosque' (Beit Hanina, 31.8290 N, 35.2254 E, 336 AH inscription)

stops.name: Nishapur, Attar writes the tenth life
stops.date_confidence: attested to the decade; the Tadhkirat al-Awliya is composed in the 1210s, and Attar dies c. 1221
stops.campa: Farid al-Din Attar, druggist and poet of Nishapur, compiles the lives of ninety-six saints and sets Ibrahim ibn Adham tenth, between Ja'far al-Sadiq at the beginning and Hallaj at the end. Four and a half centuries have gone by. Everything the world will believe about the gazelle, the shepherd's coat and the palace door is fixed in these pages and in no earlier ones that anybody can produce. The man is thin in the record and thick in Attar, and it is Attar who travels.
suggested_refs: Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya, ninety-six lives from Ja'far al-Sadiq to Mansur al-Hallaj, composed in the 1210s
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Tazkirat al-Awliya'

stops.name: Konya, Rumi puts it into verse
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Masnavi is composed across roughly 1258-1273 and the retelling is not separately dated
stops.campa: In Konya, Rumi sets the story into verse in the Masnavi at length, and it leaves prose for good. Rumi's father carried him out of Balkh as a child, ahead of the Mongols, so the family is the same city's export five centuries on. Attar is said to have met the boy at Nishapur during that flight and handed him a book. The Balkh renunciant, the Nishapur hagiographer and the Konya poet make a chain of three, and only the first of them is not certain to have existed.
suggested_refs: The Ibrahim ibn Adham passages of Rumi's Masnavi
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ibrahim ibn Adham' (Rumi's retelling in the Masnavi)

stops.name: Jableh, Ibn Battuta at the tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Rihla; the exact year of the Jableh visit is not fixed in the reachable summary, and the date shown falls within Ibn Battuta's travelling life
stops.campa: Ibn Battuta, who has been almost everywhere by this point in his life, comes through Jableh and records the tomb and mosque of Ibrahim ibn Adham as a thing a traveler stops for. Six hundred years after the death, the shrine is already an established station on the Syrian coast. His notice is the reason the Jableh claim outranks the other six in ordinary belief: somebody credible went and looked at it, and wrote down afterward that there was something standing there.
suggested_refs: Ibn Battuta's Rihla, on the tomb and mosque of Ibrahim ibn Adham at Jableh
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Jableh', citing Ibn Battuta's travel account

stops.name: London, Abou Ben Adhem
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: the poem first appears in 1834 in S. C. Hall's annual The Amulet. The 1844 date circulating in summaries is the collected Poetical Works, a decade later.
stops.campa: Leigh Hunt prints eighteen lines in an English annual about a man who wakes and finds an angel writing the names of those who love God, and asks to be set down as one who loves his fellow men, and is at the head of the list the next night. The name in the title is Ibrahim ibn Adham, worn down by a thousand years of transmission through Persian and French. English schoolchildren will recite this poem for a century without ever being told there was a man.
suggested_refs: 'Abou Ben Adhem', first printed in S. C. Hall's annual The Amulet, 1834; collected in The Poetical Works of Leigh Hunt, Edward Moxon, 1844
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Abou Ben Adhem'

stops.name: Paris, Le Memorial des saints out of a Uyghur manuscript
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Pavet de Courteille publishes Attar's book in French as Le Memorial des saints, working not from the Persian but from a Uyghur manuscript held in the Bibliotheque nationale: the lives have gone east into Central Asia and come back west again through Turkestan. Arberry will do it into English in 1966 and Losensky again in 2009. The story of the prince and the gazelle now exists in four languages, and no critical edition of any Arabic original underlies a single one of them.
suggested_refs: Pavet de Courteille, Le Memorial des saints (1889), translated from the Uyghur manuscript in the Bibliotheque nationale
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Tazkirat al-Awliya'
Correction recorded: Arberry's Muslim Saints and Mystics is 1966 (Routledge & Kegan Paul); 1979 and 1990 are reprints, and the pass gave all three years in different lenses

stops.name: New York, Flahooley and the genie
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the day shown is the Broadway opening date carried in the standard theatre record
stops.campa: A Broadway musical called Flahooley opens with a genie in it named Abou Ben Atom, played by Irwin Corey, a joke that needs the audience to know Leigh Hunt's poem, which needs the poem to have known Attar, which needs Attar to have known a story about a man at Balkh. The show closes after forty performances. The name has travelled from a garrison town under the Hindu Kush to a comedy about a wishing lamp, and has kept only its first two syllables.
suggested_refs: Flahooley (1951), book and lyrics by E. Y. Harburg and Fred Saidy, with the genie Abou Ben Atom played by Irwin Corey
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Abou Ben Adhem' (Flahooley and the character Abou Ben Atom)
